\[

\]
Their total is \(211\). Every proper subset has sum at most \(211-22=189\), while the whole list has sum \(211\). Hence no subset sum lies in \([190,210]\). Thus \(N\ge 11\).

Now consider an arbitrary permitted list. Take terms successively until their sum first becomes at least \(200\), and denote this sum by \(T\). Since the preceding sum is at most \(199\) and every term is at most \(25\),
\[
200\le T\le224.
\]
If \(T\le211\), selecting these terms gives a sum in \([189,211]\).

Suppose instead that \(212\le T\le224\), and put
\[
\ell=T-211,
\]
so \(1\le\ell\le13\). It suffices to find among the chosen terms a subcollection of sum \(r\) satisfying
\[
\ell\le r\le\ell+22,
\]
because the complementary subcollection then has sum
\[
T-r\in[189,211].
\]

Assume no such \(r\) exists. Every chosen term is then either less than \(\ell\) or greater than \(\ell+22\). Let \(C\) consist of all terms less than \(\ell\). If their total were at least \(\ell\), take a minimal initial subcollection of \(C\) whose sum is at least \(\ell\). Its sum would be at most
\[
(\ell-1)+(\ell-1)=2\ell-2\le\ell+22,
\]
contradicting the assumption. Hence the total of the terms in \(C\) is less than \(\ell\).

If \(\ell\ge3\), every term outside \(C\) would be greater than \(\ell+22\ge25\), hence at least \(26\), which is impossible. Thus all terms would lie in \(C\), but their total would be less than \(\ell\), contradicting \(T\ge212\).
